Lessons.Title: Inverse Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: understand an inverse function as undoing the original input-output process, including letter-shift ciphers and a reversible fixed-rate currency conversion; distinguish a genuine inverse from a reciprocal. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation based on Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 4 Lesson 15, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/15/preparation.html and student tasks https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/4/15/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source introduces inverses through forward/backward reasoning before abstract notation.

Original shift-cipher example: label alphabet letters with indices 0–25 and encode c=(m+3) mod26. Decode using m=(c−3) mod26, wrapping negative residues back into 0–25. For original W at index22, encoded Z index25; for X at23, encoded A index0. The same encoded letter has exactly one original letter for this fixed shift, so the mapping is invertible over the 26-letter alphabet.

Original fictitious currency desk rate: 18 pesos per one dollar at a fixed instant, with no fees. P(d)=18d pesos for dollars d≥0; the inverse process D(p)=p/18 dollars for p≥0. Ten dollars converts to180 pesos, and converting back gives 180/18=10 dollars. This is illustrative fixed arithmetic, not a current exchange-rate claim or quote.

Student activity: invent a three-letter cipher message, encode and exchange with a partner, explain why the decoding must undo the steps in reverse, then compare it with numerical conversion. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): valid bijective mapping and wrap, correct reverse operation, accurate contextual units/domains, and reasoned explanation of reversible processes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse process
KeyConcepts.Definition: An inverse takes a previous output and reconstructs the original input when possible.
KeyConcepts.Example: Multiply by18 then divide by18 restores dollars.

KeyConcepts.Title: One-to-one requirement
KeyConcepts.Definition: To have an inverse function on chosen domains, no two different inputs can share one output.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Verify uniqueness for the specified mapping.
KeyConcepts.Example: Shift by3 modulo26 permutes all 26 letters.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse versus reciprocal
KeyConcepts.Definition: Undoing f(x)=18x yields y/18, not 1/(18x) as an expression in original x.

WorkedExamples.Title: Encode and decode alphabet indices
WorkedExamples.Question: Use c=(m+3) mod26 on zero-based letter indices.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use an original function and check its rule, inverse, constraints, and units at multiple inputs.
Steps: For W, m=22 and c=(22+3) mod26=25, letter Z.
For X, m=23 and c=(23+3) mod26=0, letter A.
To decode index0, subtract3 to get −3, then wrap mod26 to23, X.
Decoding reverses encoding for both inputs.
WorkedExamples.Answer: W→Z, X→A; inverse recovers W and X.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each index stays within0–25 and the operations are reversible.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reverse a numeric conversion
WorkedExamples.Question: At fictional fixed18 pesos per dollar, convert $10 and reverse.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use an original function and check its rule, inverse, constraints, and units at multiple inputs.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain why reciprocal is different
WorkedExamples.Question: Is 1/P(d) the inverse process of P(d)=18d?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use an original function and check its rule, inverse, constraints, and units at multiple inputs.
Steps: Inverse asks for input d given output p.
Reciprocal 1/(18d) is a different function of d and is undefined at d=0.
For p=180, correct inverse returns10, not 1/180.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; the inverse process is D(p)=p/18.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring alphabet wrap in a Caesar shift
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Letters beyond Z must wrap to A.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use modulo26 with normalized nonnegative residues.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A reciprocal does not undo input-output mapping.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Solve output equation for original input.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating invented currency conversion as an actual exchange quote
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the rate as a fixed fictional teaching assumption.

SummaryPoints: Inverse functions reverse a one-to-one mapping on chosen domains.
Caesar shifts can be decoded by the opposite modular shift.
For P(d)=18d, the inverse process is D(p)=p/18.
Teacher reviews decoding and explanations; no genuine exchange-rate claim is made.
